raw_case_text: A 7 years old girl with facial edema and oliguria was diagnosed with PNS in our hospital. After 2 weeks of prednisone treatment, serum creatinine (112 mmol/L) and 24 h urinary protein (3,000 mg/m2) did not improve. Thus, patient received renal biopsy which revealed that it was minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). Subsequently, this patient received 3 consecutive days of intravenous methylprednisolone (20 mg/kg of body weight per day) pulse therapy followed by oral prednisone treatment (2 mg/kg/day) for 6 weeks and 4 times of intravenous cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2 biweekly) pulse therapy. However, complete remission was still not achieved. According to the 2021 KIDGO guidelines, the diagnosis of SRNS and acute kidney injury (AKI) at the stage 2 was established eventually. However, there were no gene mutations. For alleviating proteinuria, a single dose of rituximab (375 mg/m2) was given intravenously. Three days later, the number of CD20 positive B cell decreased to zero. Ten days later, she presented with cough, difficult breathing and fever. The chest CT showed that ground-glass opacities in both lungs (Figure 1A). Moreover, serum creatinine increased to 162 mumol/L. Pneumocystis carinii was found in sputum at the early stage by using metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) which emerges as a promising method for universal pathogens identification in the specimen due to its properties of simultaneous identification and genomic characterization of bacteria, fugus, virus and parasites. With severe respiratory failure, she was supported with mechanical ventilation. Since renal function deteriorated, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) was performed. After 24 days of intravenous caspofungin and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (SMZ-TMP) treatment, the symptoms of lung injury was improved. The chest CT showed obvious improvement of pulmonary inflammation (Figure 1B). Surprisingly, the child became sensitive to steroid and achieved complete remission in the 15 months of follow up. The percentage of CD20 positive B cells were 2.0%, 5.2%, 12.1%, 16.2% in the 3rd, 6th and 12th month respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old girl with biopsy-proven steroid-resistant minimal change nephrotic syndrome developed acute cough, difficulty breathing, and fever 10 days after receiving a single dose of intravenous rituximab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Originally admitted with facial edema, oliguria, nephrotic-range proteinuria (24-h urine protein 3,000 mg/m2), and stage 2 acute kidney injury (creatinine 112 μmol/L), the patient underwent renal biopsy confirming minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). After failing 2 weeks of oral prednisone, a 3-day IV methylprednisolone pulse (20 mg/kg/day), 6 weeks of oral prednisone (2 mg/kg/day), and four biweekly pulses of IV cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2), she was diagnosed with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS; genetic testing negative) and given a single dose of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2), which depleted her CD20+ B cells to 0% within 3 days. Ten days post-rituximab, she presented with acute cough, dyspnea, and fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Biopsy-proven minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and stage 2 acute kidney injury; status post methylprednisolone pulses, oral prednisone, four doses of IV cyclophosphamide, and single-dose rituximab (10 days prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for facial edema and oliguria; day 10 post-rituximab positive for cough, difficulty breathing, and fever.

objective.physical_examination: Severe acute respiratory failure on day 10 post-rituximab requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Renal function and proteinuria: Baseline serum creatinine 112 μmol/L and 24-h urine protein 3,000 mg/m2; at day 10 post-rituximab, serum creatinine worsened to 162 μmol/L requiring continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).
objective.advanced_workup: Renal biopsy and genetics: Minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) with negative hereditary nephrotic syndrome gene panel. Peripheral B-cell monitoring: CD20+ B cells dropped to 0% at day 3 post-rituximab (recovering to 2.0%, 5.2%, 12.1%, and 16.2% at months 3, 6, 9, and 12). Chest CT (day 10 post-rituximab): Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Sputum metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Early detection of Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) pneumonia (PCP; confirmed at an early stage by sputum metagenomic next-generation sequencing and bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest CT) complicated by acute respiratory failure and worsening acute kidney injury (creatinine 162 μmol/L) 10 days after rituximab-induced complete B-cell depletion in a 7-year-old girl with steroid-resistant minimal change nephrotic syndrome. Plan and clinical course: Managed with invasive mechanical ventilation, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), and a 24-day course of intravenous caspofungin combined with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-TMP). Her pulmonary inflammation and respiratory failure resolved completely on repeat chest CT, and she subsequently became steroid-sensitive, achieving complete nephrotic syndrome remission over 15 months of follow-up.
